$comment: The registry of subjects a document may claim authority over via `authoritative_for`.
WHY A REGISTRY AND NOT FREE TEXT
Free-text subjects cannot be validated. Two documents could each claim to be the
source of truth on authentication under slightly different spellings, and nothing
would notice. Every subject here is a closed value: verify-doc-frontmatter.mjs
fails on an unregistered subject, on two current claimants for one subject, and on
a registered subject with no claimant at all.
A subject earns an entry when exactly one document should be the place a reader
goes to be *sure* about it, and being wrong about it has a real cost. Subjects are
deliberately narrow: 'localization' would have three plausible claimants, so it is
split into the outcomes contract, the architecture contract, and the Android
implementation profile - which is why that split exists as three entries below.
Referencing a subject is always allowed. Only claiming it is controlled.

subjects.description: The versioned seller authentication contract: which auth flows are supported, their versions, and what may not change without approval.
The security properties authentication must hold regardless of implementation - token handling, session boundaries, replay and enumeration resistance.
The seller API's route-versioning and compatibility policy: what v1 guarantees, how routes are retired, what a client may rely on.
Which side wins on a sync conflict, and which data the backend is authoritative for versus the client.
Platform-agnostic localization outcomes every seller surface must satisfy - key parity, fallback behavior, RTL, dynamic-content authority.
The localization architecture decisions: default locale, supported locale set, per-app language API, bundle-split policy, translation lifecycle.
How the current Android app implements the localization contracts - resource layout, locale APIs, screenshot baselines.
The system's trust boundaries, threat model, and the controls at each boundary.
The component map: which service owns which responsibility and which data, and how requests flow between them.
Which Workers, databases, buckets, queues and hostnames exist per environment, and which repository deploys them.
How a change reaches staging and then production: gates, promotion, verification, rollback triggers and rehearsal.
The migration ledger and what each migration does. Generated from the SQL files - never hand-edited.
How to go from a fresh machine to a running local environment, and from a fresh Cloudflare account to a deployed Worker.
The backend HTTP surface: endpoints, request and response shapes, auth requirements, error semantics.
How to recover a D1 database from backup, including decryption, index and trigger rebuild, and the FTS5 caveat.
